patient.chief_complaint: Stepwise cognitive decline over 18 months with two abrupt worsenings, in a patient with a silent myocardial infarction
patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Lucia Ferraro is a 77-year-old retired seamstress who lives alone and attends with her son. He describes two abrupt worsenings over eighteen months. The first, about eighteen months ago, followed a morning when she was found confused and unable to name objects for a few hours; no medical attention was sought. The second, seven months ago, was a day of clumsiness of the left hand that lasted two days. After each event she was permanently worse: she now cannot manage her own medication, has left the door unlocked repeatedly, and no longer sews, which she had done professionally. Between the events she was stable. Her memory improves with prompting about context. Three years ago an ECG performed before a dental procedure showed an old anterior infarction that she had never known about; no echocardiogram or further cardiac assessment followed. She has no chest pain, no dyspnoea on exertion beyond her usual, and no palpitations. Her pulse is regular. She has never had documented atrial fibrillation. She is allergic to iodinated contrast. There are no hallucinations, no fluctuations and no dream enactment.

results.title: Diagnostic criteria for vascular cognitive disorders: a VASCOG statement
results.authors: Sachdev P, Kalaria R, O'Brien J, et al.
results.summary: Requires a cognitive syndrome documented on a validated instrument plus imaging or temporal evidence that cerebrovascular disease accounts for it.

results.title: Neuroimaging standards for research into small vessel disease (STRIVE-2)
results.authors: Duering M, Biessels GJ, Brodtmann A, et al.
results.summary: Defines and standardises the reporting of white matter hyperintensity, lacunes, microbleeds, perivascular spaces and cortical superficial siderosis.

vascular_cognitive_impairment.summary: No disease-modifying therapy exists for vascular cognitive impairment; management is control of the vascular risk factors, secondary prevention matched to the mechanism, review of the anticholinergic burden, and treatment of coexisting Alzheimer pathology where biomarkers support it.

medication_review.proposed: review of the current medication list for anticholinergic burden
warnings: Anticholinergic load is a reversible contributor to cognitive impairment in this population and should be quantified before any new prescription.
medication_review.summary: No prohibitive interaction identified within the current list.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Vascular dementia — multi-infarct type, cardioembolic from a left ventricular apical aneurysm with mural thrombus after an unrecognised anterior myocardial infarction

differential.key_features: A reasonable hypothesis in a multi-territory pattern, but a structural source has been demonstrated — an apical aneurysm with laminated thrombus — and the ECG shows no atrial ectopy, so further rhythm monitoring would not change management
Stepwise course with dateable events, cue-responsive recall and preserved hippocampi
Fazekas 1-2 burden is far below the threshold for attributing a dementia to small-vessel disease
No significant carotid disease, and no single artery supplies three territories across both circulations
No fever, no murmur of regurgitation beyond mild functional mitral regurgitation, no vegetation on echocardiography and no systemic features

optimal_actions.action: Obtain a collateral history from an informant who sees the patient daily: the shape of the decline (abrupt, stepwise or gradual), whether any step can be dated to a cerebrovascular event, and which instrumental activities have been lost
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Two dateable abrupt worsenings with stable plateaus between them, cue-responsive memory, loss of instrumental independence, and an unexplained silent anterior myocardial infarction never followed up

optimal_actions.action: Perform a validated bedside cognitive assessment and record the per-domain profile and whether delayed recall improves with cueing
optimal_actions.expected_finding: MoCA 20/30 with executive and attentional impairment, cue-responsive recall and mild left-sided inattention, on a stepwise history

optimal_actions.action: Order the reversible-cause screen and the vascular-risk assays that will be treated (CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate, RPR, HIV, HbA1c, lipid panel)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Reversible causes excluded; HbA1c 7.4% and LDL 106 mg/dL above target, with renal function documented for a possible anticoagulation decision

optimal_actions.action: Obtain brain MRI reported in STRIVE-2 terms — FLAIR for white matter hyperintensity with a Fazekas grade, T1/T2 for lacunes, DWI to establish that the lesions are chronic, and SWI for microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis — together with the medial temporal atrophy grade
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Three chronic infarcts across three arterial territories including the posterior circulation, with minimal white matter change and no microbleeds — an embolic pattern requiring a proximal source

optimal_actions.action: Obtain a 12-lead ECG to look for atrial fibrillation as the embolic source and for the left ventricular hypertrophy of chronic hypertension
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Sinus rhythm with Q waves of an old anterior infarction and no atrial fibrillation — the embolic question moves from rhythm to left ventricular structure

optimal_actions.action: Image the extracranial carotid arteries to establish whether a large-artery source accounts for the cortical infarcts
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Minor bilateral plaque without flow limitation, excluding a large-artery mechanism for bihemispheric infarcts

optimal_actions.action: Obtain a transthoracic echocardiogram to look for a structural cardioembolic source
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Apical left ventricular aneurysm with a mural thrombus and an ejection fraction of 38% — the embolic source, identified without any rhythm abnormality, and an indication for anticoagulation

optimal_actions.action: Confirm the diagnostic criteria applied and the current secondary-prevention targets against the guidelines
optimal_actions.expected_finding: VASCOG 2014 criteria and the 2021 AHA/ASA secondary prevention targets confirmed

optimal_actions.action: Review the medication list for anticholinergic burden and for the interaction between antithrombotic choice and the microbleed burden before prescribing
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Anticholinergic contributors identified and the antithrombotic choice reconciled with the imaging burden

optimal_actions.action: Start anticoagulation for the left ventricular thrombus and stop the aspirin unless a separate coronary indication is confirmed, refer to cardiology for assessment of the aneurysm and of heart failure therapy for an ejection fraction of 38%, intensify glycaemic and lipid control, and arrange cognitive rehabilitation with home support
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Anticoagulation started for a demonstrated structural embolic source, heart failure and aneurysm management referred, and vascular targets set

optimal_actions.action: Disclose the diagnosis and its mechanism to the patient and the informant, and address driving, medication management, finances, advance care planning and caregiver support
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Patient and informant engaged in care planning; safety domains addressed

useless_tools.rationale: EEG has no diagnostic role in vascular cognitive impairment; it belongs to the differential of a rapidly progressive or fluctuating course (Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, non-convulsive status, toxic-metabolic encephalopathy), none of which is present here

A presynaptic dopaminergic study answers the Lewy-body question, not the vascular one, and there is no spontaneous parkinsonism, no fluctuating cognition with hallucinations and no REM sleep behaviour disorder
Cardiac sympathetic imaging is a test for dementia with Lewy bodies and for autonomic failure; it says nothing about cerebrovascular disease

An untargeted paraneoplastic or autoimmune-encephalitis battery in a chronic stepwise decline with a hypertensive imaging burden is the archetypal expensive miss; the indication for those assays is a subacute multidomain syndrome
The MRI already obtained answers everything a CT could and more: CT cannot show microbleeds or cortical superficial siderosis, so it cannot grade the vascular burden this diagnosis rests on

The embolic source has been identified structurally — an apical aneurysm with mural thrombus — and the indication to anticoagulate follows from it; documenting an arrhythmia would not change the decision already made

sequence_constraints.reason: Document the cognitive deficit before attributing it: imaging read without a cognitive profile invites over-attribution of incidental white matter change

critical_actions: Establish the stepwise course and date each step
Recognise that an old anterior infarction in a patient with multi-territory brain infarcts is a structural embolic question
Obtain an ECG, and when it shows sinus rhythm with an old anterior infarct, proceed to echocardiography rather than to rhythm monitoring
Obtain brain MRI, count the infarcts by territory, and check SWI before anticoagulating
Image the carotid arteries to exclude a large-artery mechanism
Anticoagulate for the demonstrated left ventricular thrombus and stop the antiplatelet in the absence of a separate indication
Refer for heart failure management of an ejection fraction of 38%
contraindicated_actions: Do not order prolonged rhythm monitoring when a structural embolic source has already been demonstrated and the treatment decision is settled
Do not continue aspirin alongside a new anticoagulant without a specific coronary indication
Do not administer iodinated contrast studies in a patient with a documented contrast allergy without premedication and a clear indication
Do not treat this as small-vessel disease on a Fazekas 1-2 burden
Do not leave a newly identified ejection fraction of 38% unaddressed
key_reasoning_points: Cardioembolism is not synonymous with atrial fibrillation: an akinetic apical aneurysm with mural thrombus after an anterior infarct is an embolic source in a patient in sinus rhythm
The infarct distribution across both circulations forces the search for a proximal source, and the ECG points the search toward structure rather than rhythm
A silent myocardial infarction found incidentally and never investigated is the omission this case is built on — the echocardiogram it should have prompted is the study that makes the diagnosis
Once a structural source is demonstrated, rhythm monitoring adds cost without changing management
Checking SWI before anticoagulation is part of the decision, not an afterthought

red_herrings.data_point: Sinus rhythm with no history of atrial fibrillation
red_herrings.intended_effect: Concludes that there is no cardioembolic source and redirects the workup to small-vessel disease or prolonged rhythm monitoring
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The ECG carries the answer in a different form: Q waves of an old anterior infarct point to an apical aneurysm with thrombus, which echocardiography then demonstrates

red_herrings.intended_effect: Supports a diagnosis of subcortical small-vessel vascular dementia and closes the search for a source
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Fazekas 1-2 change is age-expected and cannot explain a dementia; three infarcts across both circulations can, and they require a proximal source

key_educational_points: Cardioembolic stroke does not require atrial fibrillation; left ventricular thrombus in an apical aneurysm is a structural source
An incidentally discovered silent myocardial infarction deserves an echocardiogram
The distribution of infarcts across both circulations is what makes a proximal source obligatory
Once the source is structural and demonstrated, further rhythm monitoring is waste
